newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian bourse set to oil trade in illiquid stocks.
newsitem.headline: Italian bourse set to oil trade in illiquid stocks.

text.p: The Italian stock market is set in the next two months to launch a new project to oil the mechanism for trading in very illiquid stocks, once a handful of "small cap" companies is ready to take part.

"We are technically ready. We'll start as soon as we have a minimum number of companies, at least 10, I hope in a month and a half," Francesco Cesarini, chairman of the Milan stock market council, said at a presentation on Tuesday.

The project for companies with a small market capitalisation, known as "small caps," is designed to inject liquidity into little-traded stocks through specialist operators who will trade them subject to agreement with the issuer.
The move is the latest in a series of reforms.

"Improving the liquidity of the stock exchange list is a fundamental condition for the growth of the Italian bourse which is preparing itself to face the new, competitive international environment," Cesarini said.
Some 32 intermediaries have joined the project, devised by the council, small companies and stockbroker associations.
The project's devisors have singled out 100 ordinary stocks on the bourse and over-the-counter market as likely candidates, with 34 more related stocks.

The 100 small caps and related stocks represented 1.34 trillion lire ($815 million) or just 0.9 percent of the stock market turnover of 157 trillion in 1996, with an average daily turnover per stock of 40 million lire against a market average of 1.7 billion.
On average four contracts were traded daily compared with an average of 55 for the market as a whole.
The aim is to have specialist brokers operating on the stocks who would reduce volatility and risks for investors.
Giovanni Sabatini, responsible for market organisation at bourse watchdog Consob, said the risk of price manipulation could be minimised by authorities monitoring the stocks.
The project's devisors have worked out a liquidity contract between issuers and specialists which requires specialists to buy and sell a certain amount of shares at a price differential.

The small caps -- or "in this case VERY small caps" as one senior broker put it -- will have their own trading hours, with tenders from 1145 to 1200 local time and electronic trade from 1200 to 1530 local time.
Giordano Zucchi, of small cap Italian household linen retailers Zucchi and Bassetti, attended the presentation.
"The bourse doesn't appreciate our shares. They have a market capitalisation of around 150 billion lire but the book value is around 200 to 300 billion," he said.
